```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

customers <- tibble(
  customer_id = 1:5,
  name        = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cara", "Dev", "Eli"),
  segment     = c("New", "Loyal", "Loyal", "New", "Lapsed")
)

orders <- tibble(
  order_id    = 101:107,
  customer_id = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3, 6),
  amount      = c(25, 40, 60, 15, 30, 45, 50)
)
```

## The Business Question

Our customer info and our order history live in **two separate tables**.

::: {.incremental}
- Who are our biggest spenders?
- Which segment brings in the most revenue?
- Who has never bought anything?
:::

::: {.notes}
Real business data is almost always split across related tables, so joining is a core skill.
:::

## Two Tables, One Key

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Customers**

```{r}
kable(customers)
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Orders**

```{r}
kable(orders)
```
:::
::::

Both tables share `customer_id`.

## Joining the Tables

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "2"
customer_orders <- customers |>
  left_join(orders, by = join_by(customer_id))
```

`left_join()` keeps **every customer** and adds their orders.

## Total Spend per Customer

```{r}
spend <- customer_orders |>
  group_by(name, segment) |>
  summarise(total_spend = sum(amount, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(total_spend))

kable(spend, col.names = c("Customer", "Segment", "Total Spend ($)"))
```

## Revenue by Segment

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
customer_orders |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(total_spend = sum(amount, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(segment, total_spend), y = total_spend, fill = segment)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Total spend ($)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

**Loyal** customers drive most of the revenue.

## Who Never Ordered?

```{r}
#| echo: true
customers |>
  anti_join(orders, by = join_by(customer_id))
```

. . .

Dev and Eli are a ready-made **re-engagement list**.

## Key Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
1. `left_join()` adds information while keeping every row
2. `anti_join()` finds what is missing
3. Charts and tables here are **reproducible**: they update when the data does
:::
